toc.title: "My system seems to feel safer when immobilized"
Why activation sends you back down
When it might be too much

blocks.p: I want to share a story from someone in my community who has a really good example of self-regulation. I'll keep it as anonymous and generalizable as I can, but it's a specific story from someone who is doing her own self-regulation practices. I'll call her Macy. I'll share her story, give you my thoughts on what's happening, and give you some tips for your own self-regulation practice along the way.

Macy wrote: "Thanks, Justin, for this really helpful episode. I felt like so many connections were made in my brain as I listened to it. I flip flop between shutdown, freeze, stillness and flight, fight."

That might seem like an odd sequence, but I don't think she's saying she goes from shutdown to freeze to stillness to flight to fight. It sounds like she spends a lot of time in shutdown or freeze or stillness. Those three are actually all related. Shutdown is shutdown. Freeze is shutdown plus flight or fight. And stillness is shutdown plus safety. All three involve the dorsal vagal pathways, the shutdown and immobilization pathways. In shutdown, you're immobile. In freeze, you're immobile. And in stillness, you're also immobile.
But the flavor of each is different:

ul: Shutdown immobility is limp and collapsed, with a helpless, worthless, void, cold kind of feel to it.
Freeze immobility is tense and rigid, like paralysis. You cannot move.
Stillness immobility is more relaxed and calm.

blocks.p: They're all immobile, they all feel different, and all of them have some shutdown as a part of them.

When we come out of immobility through self-regulation, we have more mobility, which is flight and fight. So Macy is saying she goes from immobility into mobility. That's definitely a good sign of self-regulation.

blocks.h: "My system seems to feel safer when immobilized"

blocks.p: Macy continued: "I am very conscious that my system seems to feel safer when immobilized. And as soon as a bit of activation arises, wham. More fear. And so back to shutdown."
"My system feels safer when immobilized" could mean a couple of different things.

It could mean someone is listening to the needs of their body. The body needs to immobilize, so they do it. That mindful listening requires some safety activation, both to notice the need and to give it to yourself without judgment. The system feeling safer through immobilizing makes sense in that way.

But when you live in shutdown or freeze, immobilizing can also be comforting because it's predictable. There might be some predictable comfort there, even though you're not mindfully experiencing it, allowing it, and opening up the potential for self-regulation. Someone in a shutdown state might say they feel safer when immobilized and then go watch TV. That's different from feeling safer when immobilized while sitting outside, feeling the sun, listening to the birds, and feeling the breeze. That's a much different experience of immobilization.

blocks.h: Why activation sends you back down

blocks.p: If you have a lot of immobilization, you need the safety state to be strengthened before you can come out of immobilization into the next step of self-regulation, which is flight and fight.

If you don't have that healthy, strong safety in your system, then as the body attempts to self-regulate out of immobility, flight and fight kick in, but there's still so much immobility that you go right back down into shutdown.

Or, as you come out of shutdown, there's a little flight or fight, but now both are active: immobility and mobility, shutdown plus flight or fight. That's freeze, or fear. So coming out of shutdown can have an element of fear to it. You come out of shutdown into flight or fight, it's too much, you're dysregulated, and you go right back down into shutdown. That's a possibility as well.
Macy wrote: "I do have a lot of fatigue in my system, and this also feeds into the fear. A fear of doing too much. So I can move to stillness, but permitting flight, fight seems just too scary."

If you're in more of a shutdown immobility, like Macy is here, I would really encourage you to focus first on stillness. Stillness is the combination of shutdown plus safety: immobilization plus connection. In stillness, you can feel relaxed, calm, and connected to the world around you, and potentially your internal world too.

So instead of trying to get from shutdown immobility into flight and fight mobility, which might be too much to ask of your system, focus on stillness. It will happen. But if you can be in stillness, then you can compassionately welcome some sympathetic energy back into your system.

If you don't have a strong enough safety state, it's going to seem scary, and you're going to have thoughts of failure: this isn't going to work. It's hopeless. Even if I access flight and fight, I'll never be able to get out of it. I don't want to live like this forever.
Your thoughts are going to go all these places. Focus on safety, safety, safety. Then safety will combine with your shutdown state, resulting in stillness.

Then Macy wrote: "After listening to this episode, I was aware of some sympathetic activation swirling around. Rather than ignoring it, I decided to mobilize, as Justin suggested. I put on some music, the techno track from the film The Outrun, made sure I was fully grounded, and let the music come into my body. I did some very strange movements. Couldn't call it dancing. Twirling around, and the dog joined in."

This is perfect. Rather than noticing sympathetic activation and trying to get rid of it, Macy welcomed it. And she did it with music. Music and movement are a perfect combination and outlet for sympathetic activation.
So it's not about noticing flight or fight coming back into your system and trying to calm it down. It's about how you welcome it: compassionately and with curiosity. That is self-regulation.

Tamping down or dampening your sympathetic activation is not self-regulation. That's dismissal. That's rejection. That's self-judgment, maybe. That's fear. And all of that makes sense. I'm not saying it's bad. It's a pretty normal part of the process. But when you focus on safety more and more, then when you feel flight or fight coming back into your system, you can do what Macy did: notice it, feel it, give it permission to be there, and give it an outlet through movement and music.

What's really cool is that she was pretty well anchored in her safety state. She used the movement and music as further safety anchoring and as a flight and fight discharge. And she had some co-regulation, because her dog joined in. That's super cool.
Irene Lyon described what safety makes room for when she was on the podcast:

q: The moment the safety comes up, what does it allow the system to do? It allows it to express all the stored stuff that has been in there forever.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: Macy went on: "I had a very strong memory of being on a roundabout as a child, being very frightened and crying, trying to get off. But in the present, my arms went up as if I was flying. It felt fabulous and freeing. I stopped as soon as I sensed a slight wave of defensive energy." And the thought she had was, "This might be too much."

That's a really good breakdown of all the pieces: the safety anchoring pathways, the co-regulation, the Polyvagal knowledge. And she broke down her state, sensation, impulse, emotion, and cognition. Really, really good job, Macy.

So why did this memory come into Macy's mind? She was successfully self-regulating, and story follows state. The thoughts in our brain, whether they're words, images, beliefs, or memories, follow the state of our body.

There may be a moment in time that left an imprint on your body, and it could be a traumatizing one. That's what's going to come up as you self-regulate, or as you feel things in the present moment that are reminiscent of the past. For Macy, the sympathetic activation coming up within her was reminiscent of the roundabout as a child. It sounds like that moment left an imprint on her of some kind.

As new feelings, emotions, and sensations come into our body, or returning ones come back, our thoughts follow. They remember or conjure up the thing that once happened way back when, or the thing somebody said when you were little. Your story follows the state of your nervous system. In a safety state, your thoughts will be more flavored by safety. In a sympathetic state, your thoughts will be sympathetically flavored, and that might include memories.

What Macy did is a really good example of how I think about, teach, and work with my clients. My clients can talk with me about past events, even past traumatic events. That's totally fine. The past always comes up.

But I work in the present moment. My focus is pretty much entirely on what's happening right here and right now. Even as we're talking about the past: how do we feel about it right here, right now? As we do these self-regulation practices, memories of the past come up, and then that event all of a sudden becomes much more relevant.

So rather than fishing for past traumatic events, parental issues, or past relationship issues, I focus on the here and now. Then, as it's relevant, as you self-regulate: "Oh yeah, there was that thing that happened when I was a kid." "Oh yeah, I do have this history of these types of relationships." Your brain starts to remember, or put things together in a much different way.

So if that's your focus, keep doing it. Focus on the present moment. Your body will tell you what it needs. Listen to it. As you do those self-regulation practices, your brain will remember, or maybe have a new thought, maybe a more hopeful one. Memories might be part of what comes up.

Macy said, "In the present, my arms went up as if I was flying." She had an impulse, she listened to it, and she let her body complete that impulse in the present moment. That was really good. It felt fabulous. It felt freeing.

It was the same sympathetic energy, or similar enough, with a different outcome. It wasn't defense. It wasn't out of control. She wasn't lost or overwhelmed as a kid. She was in the present moment as an adult, feeling and experiencing it with her safety state firmly anchored. And that unlocked all the self-regulation that unfolded from there.

blocks.h: When it might be too much

blocks.p: She stopped as soon as she sensed a slight wave of defensive energy, and the thought was, "This might be too much." That's totally fine. You might reach a point where it feels like too much, and your brain says this might be too much.
You have two options:

ol: Pause. Listen to it, rest, recover, and come back to it later. That's totally fine.
Tiptoe a bit further. If you're up for it, you can say, "No, I can handle this," and feel a little more into whatever new defensive wave is coming up.

blocks.p: I don't want anyone to end up in further dysregulation and retraumatize themselves. If it starts to feel like overwhelm or fear, that's probably a pretty good indication it's too much. But if there's some safety, some "yes, I can do this" left within you, I think it's okay to take another step. You don't have to, but it's an option.

Macy also asked, "Justin, could you consider covering how to move into feeling safe with sympathetic activation?" That is the next step: how do we welcome sympathetic activation with compassion and use it, just like Macy did here?

Macy, seriously, incredible. Great job, and thank you so much for sharing this self-regulation story. I love seeing the changes people go through, and hearing from people who are finding success through present moment mindfulness practices, through Polyvagal Theory knowledge, and then building on it.
